Some legacy assets might still be required to ensure power capacity and reliability in areas where advanced fuel supplies are not yet readily available or where environmental factors such as extreme temperatures reduce the performance of some advanced energy technologies. DOW will likely see higher direct costs from maintaining or upgrading legacy 11 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. infrastructure while expanding advanced energy assets, including replacement parts and fueling infrastructure. The initial expense of a resilient energy system can slow the adoption timeline, with procurement categorized into time-phased pieces or structured by funding types (e.g., financed and appropriated portions), which introduces complexities and delays into deployment timelines. These segmented approaches can make system integration more difficult. Ensuring the parallel functionality of legacy and new systems will likely require hybrid solutions to bridge gaps, especially in remote or harsh environments where new energy supplies might be variable (e.g., during winter in polar regions where EV battery performance is less optimal or where solar energy is insufficient). Hybrid arrangements will still require new support systems, including EV charging infrastructure, cybersecurity support, and battery disposal (Tegler 2025). Beyond the added cost of maintaining multiple supply lines, these systems introduce greater maintenance complexity. Support personnel will need expertise not only in internal combustion engines, but also in electronics and energy storage that may require additional training and resources. Delays in adjusting DOW plans for bridging gaps could result in power shortfalls. If the adoption of advanced energy technologies in some operational theaters moves more quickly than DOW’s standard timelines for equipment lifespans, legacy equipment and infrastructure could become stranded assets that become economically unviable before their anticipated lifespan is over due to changes in the market, technology, or regulations. For example, heavy machinery and handling equipment staged at military airfields worldwide have a useful life of 5,000 to 12,000 hours depending on the equipment type and maintenance (Louisiana CAT 2023), and internal combustion engine vehicles are likely to be functional for decades, according to an interviewee. Maintaining battlefield strength would then incur higher- than-anticipated costs, and contingency planning for such cases will be crucial for DOW to prepare for potential budgetary needs. Moreover, stranded assets could become unexpected costs or liabilities for DOW. Depending on their location, DOW may be responsible for proper disposal.
